claims.text: The target material is a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
A brief rapid ultrahigh-temperature liquid-phase-assisted sintering treatment can create a transient eutectic liquid at W–Cu interfaces.
A minor additive or an optimized temperature ramp could induce the transient interfacial liquid in W–Cu.
The treatment should use brief ultrahigh-temperature exposure followed by rapid cooling.
The transient liquid fills interfacial voids in the W–Cu composite.
Upon solidification, the transient liquid forms a crystalline interfacial phase bridging W and Cu.
The transient liquid enhances wetting between tungsten and copper.
Enhanced wetting and liquid filling mitigate W–Cu phase separation and interfacial void formation.
Solidification after liquid-phase sintering produces stronger W–Cu interfacial bonding.
The stronger interface prevents microstructural degradation under thermal and irradiation stresses.
The treated W–Cu composite will have measurably higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite under operational heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Conventionally processed untreated W–Cu composites typically exhibit phase separation and interfacial voids that degrade thermal conductivity.
The intervention remains beneficial during high heat transfer and irradiation typical of joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components.

contradictions.description: The design specifies laser-flash analysis, which is a transient diffusivity method, while the measurements specify thermal conductivity under steady-state conditions; the intended thermal test protocol is therefore internally inconsistent.
